newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Shares mixed, mark weak, markets eye Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Shares mixed, mark weak, markets eye Greenspan.

text.p: Major European bourses put on a mixed performance on Wednesday ahead of further comments by the head of the U.S. central bank, who has spooked investors on various occasions with cautionary comments on trading levels.
An overnight drop on Wall Street helped undermine share prices in London and Paris. But the Frankfurt bourse topped records set in late electronic business on Tuesday.

On currency markets, the dollar traded a little below a new 34-month peak against the German currency of 1.7169 marks, hit in Asian business, but lost some ground against a firm Japanese yen at around 121.40 yen.

Traders said comments on Tuesday by Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm that recent mark movements were still an "appropriate correction" lessened the attraction of the mark, already depressed by weakness in the German economy.
"Generally poor sentiment toward the mark remains and Palm's comments seemed to give its recent bout of weakness a pat on the back," said Peter Wood, currency trader at Bank of Boston.
Gold traded around $356, down almost $4 from the previous London close, after news that the Swiss government and central bank plan to revalue official gold reserves to create a humanitarian fund.
On the oil market, prices continued a recent recovery with April futures for Brent blend up 18 cents at $19.68 a barrel.

The main focus for markets was two speeches by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan -- starting with comments on the consumer price index from 1230 GMT and then the second leg of his Humphrey Hawkins Congressional testimony at 1900 GMT.

The London stock market, Europe's busiest, opened lower after a 66-point fall in the Dow Jones industrial average in New York and in reaction to some disappointing corporate results which took the shine off Tuesday's record-breaking performance.
"We are suffering from a combination of Wall Street and pre-Greenspan nerves," one dealer said. "There is no selling pressure but buyers have been pretty thin on the ground too."
In the first half of his testimony a week ago, Greenspan sent stocks tumbling with a warning that Wall Street's rise had "raised questions of sustainability".
Markets will be watching for clarification of this remark and any clues on interest rates. In separate comments on Tuesday, Greenspan said he was not trying to push stock market prices lower.
"These are very thick, elaborate, international markets which are driven by decisions of millions of people," Greenspan said. "Nobody can affect them in a fundamental way."
Traders and investors were unsure what to think and analysts noted Greenspan has said he is ready to raise interest rates to contain inflation.
Greenspan had been using a tactic of "verbal tightening" in order to condition the market for higher rates later this year, said Trevor Greeton, global strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.
"People will be nervous today with Greenspan coming up," one London share dealer said. "People will all be watching him, rather than Ken and Eddie."

British Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George held their monthly monetary meeting on Wednesday but, as expected this close to an election due by May, the central bank left official interest rates unchanged.
Among key London share movements, tobacco-to-insurance conglomerate B.A.T. slipped 20-1/2 pence to 529 after news of an unexpected charge for reserves against U.S. environmental claims.

In Frankfurt shares showed no signs of hangover from Tuesday's record-breaking run, boosted by a steady dollar, which is good news for German exporters and outweighed the effect of Wall Street's drop.
French shares pared their losses after opening lower in line with Wall Street, but Renault was down 3.45 percent at 137 francs amid the fear of a backlash to its plant closure plans.

In currencies, comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that a strong dollar was in U.S. interests but that it had been strong for "quite some time" and that the United States was watching the trade deficit with Japan gave support to the yen.

Chief Tokyo government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama, meanwhile, said Japan needed to consider how to deal with the impact that low interest rates have on incomes -- making the market more nervous about how long Japanese interest rates can remain low, traders said.

"Even if we don't see the Bank of Japan hiking rates before the Fed does, interest rate expectations will still remain at the margin and not move further in favour of the dollar (against the yen)," Claudio Demolli, currency analyst at Merrill Lynch in London, said.
CURRENCIES AT 1230 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 1.7140 marks and 121.38 yen, compared with 1.7118 and 121.94 in late European trade on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1100 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 15.8 points at 4,341.9.
PARIS - The CAC-40 lost 2.42 points at 2,649.27.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index gained 42.33 points to a record 3,362.99 in late floor trading.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold traded around $356.35 an ounce after a morning fix of $355.75, down from the previous London close of $359.80. Silver slipped four cents to $5.21.
